# Static electricity, conductors and insulators, Leyden jar (`static_electricity`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: helped by glassmaking
- Core idea: Rubbing glass with silk, or amber, sulphur or resin with wool or fur, charges them so that they attract chaff and give small sparks. There are two kinds of charge: like repels like, unlike attract. Metals, water and the human body conduct charge away; glass, silk, wax, resin and dry air do not, so a conductor keeps its charge only if it hangs on silk or stands on glass or wax. A glass globe or cylinder turned on an axle against a leather pad is a continuous source, and a glass jar lined inside and outside with metal foil (Leyden jar) stores enough charge for a strong spark and shock. Lightning is the same thing on a large scale.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying it in damp weather: a film of moisture on the glass leaks the charge away and nothing works
  - Treating the Leyden jar as a toy; a large jar or a battery of jars gives shocks that can injure or kill
  - Saying that static and current electricity are different things; it is the same charge, at high tension and tiny quantity
  - Believing a static machine can drive a telegraph, lamp or motor; it delivers almost no continuous current
  - Claiming that the ancients understood electricity; they knew only that rubbed amber attracts light things
- History: greece: c. 600 BC – attraction by rubbed amber (elektron) is attributed to Thales by later writers; c. 300 BC Theophrastus mentions it for another stone; china: 1st c. AD – Wang Chong, Lunheng, compares dunmou picking up mustard seeds with a lodestone drawing needles. The passage does not describe rubbing; europe: 1600 – Gilbert separates electric from magnetic attraction; c. 1660 Guericke's sulphur globe; 1706 Hauksbee's glass globe machine; 1729 Gray, conduction; 1733 Du Fay, two kinds of electricity; 1745–1746 Leyden jar (Kleist, Musschenbroek); americas: 1747–1750 – Franklin in Philadelphia: one fluid, plus and minus, conservation of charge, power of points
- Read:
  - Wang Chong, Lunheng, Luan long and Zao hu (1st c. AD)
  - William Gilbert, De Magnete (1600)
  - J. L. Heilbron, Electricity in the 17th and 18th Centuries (1979)
